claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC random solid-solution alloy.
Processing may leave nanoscale precipitates or dislocation networks in the initial microstructure.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate above 700°C.
High-temperature strain-rate insensitivity is caused by dynamic recovery and recrystallization becoming dominant over dislocation glide.
At room temperature, yield strength is highly strain-rate sensitive.
Room-temperature strain-rate sensitivity arises from deformation twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation mechanisms.
Low-temperature plastic deformation involves nucleation and motion of partial dislocations.
Partial-dislocation activity provides a dislocation-based route to yielding under tension.
Low-temperature deformation produces deformation twins, stacking-fault networks, Lomer-Cottrell locks, and HCP martensite.
FCC-to-HCP transformation can proceed through the introduction or accumulation of stacking faults.
Above approximately 700°C, the deformation microstructure shifts from slip and twinning to slip and recrystallization.
Dynamic recovery and recrystallization allow dislocations to annihilate and rearrange rapidly at high temperature.
Yield strength decreases from about 750 MPa at 25°C to about 220 MPa at 900°C.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent is high at room temperature and approaches zero above 700°C.
A stacking-fault energy that permits twinning and phase transformation at low temperature but recovery at high temperature is a boundary condition for the hypothesis.
A high volume fraction of thermally stable precipitates could invalidate the proposed high-temperature behavior by pinning dislocations.
The transition temperature can vary with composition, grain size, precipitate distribution, and solute-dependent recovery activation energy.
A greater than 5% increase in yield strength at 800°C when strain rate rises from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-1 s^-1 is defined as falsifying high-temperature strain-rate insensitivity.
Accumulation of HCP phase or deformation twins at 800°C correlated with higher high-rate flow stress would contradict the proposed dominance of dynamic recovery.
